title: General Motors Shares Plunge 6% Despite $20 Billion Buyback Announcement And Earnings Beat
desc:
General Motors Shares Plunge 6% Despite $20 Billion Buyback Announcement And Earnings Beat

General Motors shares are plunging more than 6% in premarket trading Tuesday, despite the automaker announcing a massive new $20 billion share repurchase program and reporting quarterly earnings that came in ahead of Wall Street expectations, according to Bloomberg News.

The selling comes as GM continues to grapple with a weakening U.S. auto market, where higher financing costs and pressure on household budgets have made it increasingly difficult to sell lower-priced vehicles. Demand for the company's more expensive trucks and SUVs has held up considerably better, allowing GM to preserve profitability even as overall sales volumes come under pressure.

Bloomberg/Financial Post reports that for the third quarter, GM generated approximately $50 billion in revenue and $4.1 billion in adjusted operating profit, narrowly beating analyst expectations. Adjusted earnings of $3.70 per share also exceeded the $3.56 consensus estimate. Perhaps more importantly, automotive free cash flow jumped 40% to $5.9 billion.

That cash generation is helping fund an increasingly aggressive effort to return money to shareholders. GM's latest $20 billion repurchase authorization follows a $6 billion program announced earlier this year and approximately $29.5 billion in buybacks completed since 2023. The newest authorization is expected to be used over several years.

Management also tightened its 2026 earnings forecast, now expecting adjusted operating profit between $14.5 billion and $15.5 billion, versus its previous projection of $14 billion to $16 billion. The midpoint of the guidance remains unchanged.

Looking ahead, GM is putting additional emphasis on its bread-and-butter pickup business, with redesigned Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra trucks expected later this year. The company also plans to increase output of higher-end models equipped with V-8 engines, betting that wealthier consumers will continue paying a premium for larger vehicles.

The approach marks a notable change from GM's previous enthusiasm for electric vehicles and autonomous driving, both of which have resulted in expensive setbacks. CEO Mary Barra has increasingly redirected attention toward established profit centers, while pursuing more targeted opportunities in vehicle software, advanced driver assistance and even defense-related manufacturing.

GM's overseas operations, meanwhile, continue to struggle. Quarterly profit from China fell 60% from a year earlier to just $32 million.

The broader auto industry has undergone a significant reassessment over the past two years. After spending much of the early 2020s promising an accelerated transition to electric vehicles, several major manufacturers have scaled back EV investments, delayed launches and absorbed substantial losses as consumer adoption failed to match earlier expectations.

At the same time, persistently expensive vehicles, elevated interest rates and increasingly stretched consumers have complicated the outlook for traditional auto sales. The result is an industry increasingly focused on protecting margins, generating cash and selling the vehicles customers are actually willing to buy, rather than pursuing the ambitious growth narratives that dominated the sector just a few years ago.

title: UK Sends Typhoon Jets To Support Saudis Amid Houthi Attacks

UK Sends Typhoon Jets To Support Saudis Amid Houthi Attacks

The United Kingdom has on Tuesday announced yet more creeping escalation in the Yemen war. It is offering Saudi Arabia 'defensive' assistance by deploying its Typhoon fighter jets.

The British Ministry of Defence claimed the warplanes and British pilots would operate only in a "defensive role" - though its yet to be seen what exactly this will mean.

"The UK will fly defensive counter air missions to support the protection of Saudi cities and critical national infrastructure against aerial attack, using RAF Typhoon fighter jets," the statement added.

In this current situation the line between what gets deemed defensive vs. offensive is going to be thin, at a moment Saudi territory has been coming under almost daily attack from Houthi ballistic missiles and drones. Will UK warplanes move to take out launch systems if their locations are identified in Yemen?

The kingdom's major airports have been shuttered for the past week, with airspace effectively closed due to the missile threat, and Aramco energy sites have been pummeled.

It is almost unprecedented to see the Saudi economy, which relies heavily on foreign investments for expansion, essentially get temporarily cut off from the outside world. The kingdom has been forced to cancel over a dozen major events it was expected to host, including its annual 'Davos in the Desert' flagship investor conference, which was originally scheduled for next week.

Concerning the kingdom's Future Investment Initiative, The Wall Street Journal reported that "Organizers decided Monday that if the conference goes ahead, its sessions will be held virtually rather than in person, the people said."

The report added: "The kingdom is expected to make a decision Tuesday or earlier whether to postpone the event, they said. Postponement is the most likely outcome, some of the people said."

title: EU NatGas Hits 2022 Crisis Levels As Goldman Warns 150 Euros Could Be Next
desc:
EU NatGas Hits 2022 Crisis Levels As Goldman Warns 150 Euros Could Be Next

Back in late August, Goldman Sachs commodities expert Samantha Dart warned that EU natural gas prices would need to soar dramatically to discourage Asian LNG demand and shift cargoes to Europe amid disruptions at the Strait of Hormuz.

*EUROPE'S GAS BENCHMARK EXCEEDS €90 FOR FIRST TIME SINCE 2022

— zerohedge (@zerohedge) October 20, 2026

Fast forward to Tuesday morning, European gas prices (TTF) have topped 90 euros per megawatt-hour, the highest level since late 2022. Notably, Dart warned about where prices were headed when EU NatGas was trading around 67 euros.

Separately, Goldman's Daan Struyven and Dart released a new note earlier today, putting their base case for Brent crude at $90 a barrel and European benchmark EU NatGas at 70 euros by year-end, assuming a recovery in Middle Eastern supply and easing risk premiums. Brent is forecast to average $80 in 2027.

However, they warned that risks remained skewed toward the upside: Brent crude could climb to $140 early next year and average about $125 in 2027 if Gulf oil output averages 5 million barrels a day below February 2026 levels. As for EU NatGas, they warned it could soar to 150 euros if Gulf LNG exports remain at just one quarter of normal levels and a more severe winter boosts heating demand.

Here's what they said:

Our base case is that a further recovery in Mideast supply and a moderation in the risk premium reduce prices of Brent crude and European natural gas to $90/bbl and EUR70/MWh, respectively, by end-2026.2 However, we remain concerned that geopolitical escalation—such as intensified shipping attacks or damage to energy infrastructure—and, for European natural gas, a cold winter could push energy prices significantly higher.

While estimated Persian Gulf exports of crude oil—including estimated dark exports— remained near their 2025 average over the past 7 days (Exhibit 2), they edged down from the early October highs as attacks on ships attempting to cross Hormuz have picked up (Exhibit 2). Estimated Gulf exports of refined oil products are much lower at around 40% of the 2025 average, in part reflecting Mideast refinery outages. Similarly, visible LNG crossings through Hormuz, have edged down this month relative to late October levels.

Misses in Mideast supply could push energy prices significantly higher:

  • Brent might rally to $140 in early 2027 and average around $125/bbl in 2027 (red line, Exhibit 4) if 2027 average Gulf output remains 5mb/d below Feb26 levels (while refined product prices would likely rise further from already very high levels)
  • TTF might rally to 150 EUR/MWh by year-end if Persian Gulf LNG exports don't improve beyond 25% of normal and if the winter realizes 1 std. dev. colder than average (Exhibit 5)

Beyond energy, the analysts noted that the Bloomberg Commodity Index delivered a 36% total return this year, outperforming equities and bonds.

As ex-Goldman Sachs Jeff Currie, including ourselves, has pointed out, commodities have entered a period of scarcity, whether due to resource nationalism, adverse weather, supply woes, and more.

US futures are lower, led by the Nasdaq, as Monday's AI relief bounce fizzled overnight after South Korean data-center firm Elice cratered more than 30% in its trading debut, reviving doubts about who exactly will earn a return on the AI capex binge, while OpenAI is reportedly rushing to raise about $30 billion ahead of Anthropic's IPO and French stress returned with a vengeance; as a result the OAT-Bund spread widened to a 151bps peak, swiftly approaching the 152bps high from just after the draft budget was presented. In premarket trading, Mag 7 names are mostly lower (AAPL -0.9%, META -0.4%, NVDA -0.4%), while levered AI names like CoreWeave and Nebius give back some of Monday's gains. The day's driver is AI (again): The spectacular collapse of Korean neocloud Elice, which as we flagged last night plunged 30% minutes after IPOing, hit chip-heavy Asian markets hardest with the Kospi tumbling 3.65% and Hynix slumping, and with the Fed in blackout ahead of the Oct. 28 FOMC, tech earnings are the only game in town this week. Treasuries are marginally firmer with the 10Y yield down 2bps at 5.12%, tracking a haven bid in Bunds even as French OATs underperform and Gilts lag after a hawkish UK jobs report. The dollar is modestly weaker, with the DXY in a 101.74-101.98 range and cable rising after UK unemployment unexpectedly fell to 4.7%. Brent holds above $110/bbl near a five-month high and European gas is back near €90/MWh, gold slips toward the bottom of its $4,116-4,147 range and copper hovers around $14,400/t. Bitcoin is choppy around $81-82k. In other corporate news, OpenAI is reportedly rushing to lock in investor commitments for a roughly $30 billion private round, with SoftBank and MGX in talks, before rival Anthropic's expected mid-November IPO; the raise could value OpenAI above $1.4 trillion and the company is pitching annualized revenue of $50 billion, which it expects to hit $70 billion by year-end (nothing says "no bubble here" like racing to get your round done before the competition lists). ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent have ordered more than 3 million of Nvidia's export-compliant RTX PRO 5500 GPUs worth over $35 billion. Amazon plans to invest €16 billion in Germany in 2027 after Chancellor Merz said Berlin aims to quadruple AI compute capacity by 2030, and Business Insider reports Amazon is buying billions of dollars of GPUs and parking them in inventory while it waits for data center capacity to come online. Broadcom signed a 10-year cloud infrastructure agreement with Japan's NTT Docomo; Waymo reportedly plans a fleet of 20,000 vehicles by the end of 2027; and Micron's Taiwan union may strike Thursday over a bonus dispute.

Monday's tech bounce was always going to need confirmation, and overnight it got the opposite. Elice, a Korean neocloud whose KRW201bn IPO was, don't laugh, "more than 400x subscribed", fell as much as 33% on its debut, a reminder that the IPO was priced before the AI selloff and that the market's appetite for levered AI infrastructure has not come back (as we discussed in The AI Canary, the buyers in Korea have disappeared). The result: de-rating of AI and crowded growth trades continued to dominate Asian price action, with the Kospi down 3.65% and back below 5,600, while Nasdaq futures handed back a chunk of yesterday's gains.

“What they’re questioning is whether every dollar of AI capex earns more than it costs to finance,” said Ninghui Liu, head of investment strategy and research for APAC at State Street Investment Management.

“The weekend’s protests have further intensified concerns about French public finances,” said Pia Fromlet, an economist at SEB.

Under the surface, Monday was hardly a ringing endorsement either. JPM's Market Intel desk notes that equities rebounded on muted volumes and with little sign of broad participation; equal weight lagged and most of tech's gains came premarket with limited follow-through. JPM TMT trader Brian Heavey was blunter: "We are NOT seeing any real demand in the AI complex, this feels like a technical over sold bounce after last week's wipeout," pointing out that CRWV traded flat after indicating +8% on the Goldman upgrade. His punchline: "Capital markets hold the keys to capex levels going forward." Andrew Tyler's team nonetheless stays Tactically Bullish, preferring cyclicals outside tech and selectively buying Semis and Memory weakness via defined-risk options.

Goldman's desks see the de-risking as largely done but the rotation as unfinished. Per GS Prime data relayed by the Asia sales desk, US L/S net leverage fell 3.2pts last week, the largest weekly drop since Liberation Day, with Info Tech seeing the largest net selling and de-grossing on record, while the HF VIP basket had its worst week since Covid. At the same time retail went the other way, with a record $7 billion pouring into SOXL, as we detailed over the weekend. Goldman's Sam Dunn described Monday as a "calm start to the week with a relief rally ... that felt like a cessation of the high-velocity supply," with floor activity "a 3 on a 1-10 scale," while the bank's chart of the day shows the AI winners vs AI at risk pair is now flat on the year after rising some 100% in the first half. And with an early Q3 read showing only 53% of firms beating EPS by more than one standard deviation (vs a 64% four-quarter average), GS's Dani Wojdyla notes "the next market move is largely dependent on earnings confirmation."

Credit remains the pressure point. The FT reports investors are racing to buy credit default swaps to protect portfolios in case the AI boom unravels, CoreWeave CDS remains above 1,000bps per Newsquawk, and Goldman notes AI-related HY spreads widened 25bps vs just 2bps for non-AI issuers. Recall that Morgan Stanley warned that AI's $1.6 trillion capex plan now lives or dies in the credit market, and Goldman quietly shifted its credit preference toward BBBs as AI debt floods every corner of the market.

In Europe, the French story is back. The 10Y OAT yield jumped 13.4bps to 4.93% on Monday, its highest close since 2002, and the OAT-Bund spread widened again today to a 156bps peak even after protests subsided following tighter security measures and curfews. Goldman's Alexandre Stott expects the budget to be adopted this year, with Finance Minister Lescure saying the government would take "the unprecedented step of using ordinances to bypass Parliament altogether" if needed, but GS's poll-based model still sees Le Pen as the clear favorite for 2027. Moody's is expected to downgrade France on Friday; JPM's EGB desk thinks it is priced in.

In Europe, the Stoxx 600 is down 0.6%, falling for a second day after nearly a 1% drop on Monday, not helped by the risk tone in Asia and several disappointing company updates. Health care tops the sector pile, followed by personal care and food & beverage, while industrials, tech and basic resources lag. Chip names are hit hardest, with ASML and ASMI each down more than 3% and JPM's European Semis basket down 3.3%, alongside its Ceasefire, China Exposure and Software baskets among the worst performers. The DAX and Euro Stoxx 50 underperform after a weak ZEW, where the German expectations index dropped to 28.1 vs 30 expected, while German PPI surged 6.7% y/y.

Asian stocks were mostly lower despite the rebound on Wall Street, as the region failed to sustain the AI-led recovery. South Korea's Kospi slumped 3.65% with roughly 86% of names lower, as foreigners net sold $255 million of tech including $296 million of SK Hynix, amid reports that US big tech is pushing for lower memory prices by citing Chinese suppliers. Japan's Nikkei fell 1.3% and the Topix 1.4%, with SoftBank, Tokyo Electron and Advantest accounting for about 60% of the Nikkei's decline; Goldman notes the Topix broke its CTA short-term threshold again, implying around $1.1 billion of CTA selling this week, while Japanese banks fell 4.3% after a strong 20-year JGB auction. The Hang Seng dropped 1.3% as it returned from holiday, with Lenovo down 10% and CATL down 6.6%, while the CSI 300 fell 0.5% after China held its loan prime rates for a 17th month. Taiwan's Taiex fell 1.1% and Australia's ASX 200 slipped 0.4%. The exception was Indonesia, where the JCI soared 5.3% after a two-day crash of about 15%, the steepest since 1989 (more here).

In FX, the dollar is modestly softer, with the DXY in a 101.74 to 101.98 range and the low of the day coinciding with its 21-DMA. Sterling is the story after a better than expected UK jobs report, with unemployment falling to 4.7% vs 4.9% expected, lifting cable from 1.3328 to 1.3358 and bolstering the case for a BoE hike in November. The kiwi and loonie outperform, the latter on bets the BoC hikes next week (about 80% priced, up from about 40% last week), while the euro is flat and the only G10 currency failing to gain against the dollar as the OAT-Bund spread widens. The yen is little changed after Reuters reported the BoJ will likely hold in October but could signal a December hike.

In rates, Treasuries are slightly firmer, holding within Monday's ranges, with the 10Y yield about 2bps lower at 5.12% after Monday's jump of nearly 7bps; JPM sees 2s flat and 5s, 10s and 30s about 1bp lower, with no overt flattening or steepening bias. Bunds outperform, rallying about 3bps on a modest haven bid from the tepid Asian risk tone, while French OATs lag as the OAT-Bund spread widens to 151bps ahead of Moody's Friday review, and gilts slip after the hawkish jobs data. In Japan, a strong 20-year JGB auction (5.84x bid-to-cover vs 4.01x prior) boosted JGBs. With the Fed in blackout ahead of the Oct. 28 FOMC, the focus is on tech earnings and geopolitics (in a market where the 10Y sits above 5%, apparently that passes for calm).

In commodities, crude is choppy but holds near the top of its range: Brent trades above $111/bbl in a $109.00-111.75 range, near a five-month high, while WTI briefly topped $100 ($98.04-100.93). Iran's IRGC said two oil tankers struck naval mines along the southern route of the Strait of Hormuz and that it downed a US MQ-9 drone, while Pakistan's Army Chief arrived in Tehran for talks and the Iranian Foreign Ministry struck a conciliatory tone. IEA chief Birol said the agency will consider releasing more emergency stocks if needed. Dutch TTF gas is climbing again in a €87.60-89.80/MWh range. I wanted to start by highlighting yesterday’s CoTD “Different Ways to Skin Capex”, partly as it took me a long time to do, and partly as the graphs may not have been easy to read on email. Hopefully with the link to the piece on the DBRI site here, they’re slightly easier to read. The key divide from the main chart is that over the last year the gap has increased between those writing the enormous AI capex cheques and those cashing them in. Many of the big spenders have gone sideways, while the physical bottlenecks in memory, storage, chip packaging and networking have been the big winners. There is a second striking split between “atoms” and “bits”, with Asian hardware names surging as software and Indian IT services have lagged, alongside sharp falls among some of the more leveraged AI build-outs. Apple and Alphabet are notable mega-cap exceptions, but for different reasons — Apple because it has largely avoided the data-centre capex arms race, and Alphabet because it is increasingly demonstrating that heavy AI spending can translate into revenue. The broader conclusion is that investors are no longer simply investing in Big Tech or AI in aggregate: they are investing in Big Tech’s budgets, while becoming much more discriminating about who ultimately earns an adequate return from them. See the short note for more. I think it breaks things down nicely.

It’s been another eventful 24 hours for markets, with a bunch of competing narratives for investors to grapple with. On the bright side, the AI selloff began to stabilise, with the Philly semiconductor index (+1.61%) finally breaking a run of 8 consecutive declines. There's been considerable volatility elsewhere as well, as the stress around French assets returned after the weekend unrest. And matters weren’t helped by another rise in European natural gas prices, which moved up to a post-2022 high of €88.04/MWh. So that fuelled the broader economic concerns around the continent, with equities including the STOXX 600 (-0.80%) posting sharp declines.

We’ll start with the French story, as that created the biggest market moves over the session, with the negativity clear from the open. The impact was most obvious for the country’s sovereign debt, with 10yr French OAT yields up +13.4bps on the day to 4.93%, their highest closing level since 2002. Moreover, because Germany’s 10yr bund yields were “only” up +2.9bps on the day to 3.45%, that pushed the 10yr OAT-bund spread up to 148bps by the close. Admittedly, it wasn’t quite as high as the intraday peak above 150bps earlier this month, so we haven’t returned to peak stress yet. But after two weeks when the spread had broadly stabilised, the concerns were clearly picking back up in yesterday’s session. Indeed, it was a similar story for the 2yr spread as well, which also jumped up +6.6bps on the day to 54bps.

Those market concerns around French debt cascaded across other countries and asset classes too. For instance, the Italian 10yr spread over bunds was also up +4.7bps on the day to 111bps, whilst Spain’s was up +1.2bps to 62bps. Meanwhile in equities, the STOXX Banks index (-2.07%) hit a 4-month low, and there were even bigger declines for the French banks, including Société Générale (-3.41%), Crédit Agricole (-2.64%) and BNP Paribas (-2.48%). And in turn, all that caused fresh pressure for the Euro itself, which weakened -0.23% against the US Dollar to close at $1.1213. The Euro is back up +0.17% this morning as the unrest in France didn't continue overnight after strict curfews and other measures were implemented across the country.

Yesterday's news out of Europe was exacerbated by the latest moves in energy prices, which added to concerns around inflation and further ECB rate hikes. Most strikingly, the front-end natural gas future (+0.56%) rose to €88.04/MWh, which is another post-2022 high, and now leaves it up +21.7% in October alone. So that led investors to price in more inflation, with the 1yr Euro inflation swap (+11.3bps) up to 3.80%, its highest since May.

Oil prices did stabilise but Brent crude (-0.28% top $109.55/bbl) still settled within touching distance of Friday’s 5-month high. Brent had pulled back towards $107/bbl early on Monday, helped by some talk on the wires that US and Iran had reached a breakthrough in mediations that would be announced later in the week. However, the fact that this got very little airtime reflects that markets have heard this story before and will take a lot to believe it. The respite indeed proved short-lived, with oil prices jumping higher around the European close as Iran’s First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said that Iran has “no choice but to exercise sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz”. So that added to the sense that a deal before the US midterms in two weeks’ time is going to be challenging, while investors are also concerned that the US administration may be more likely to escalate against Iran after the midterms as Iran’s increased strikes in Hormuz have now slowed the increase in oil flows through Hormuz that had emerged over the previous couple of months. Perhaps reflecting that, the longer-dated futures continued to climb, with 12-month Brent futures (+0.14%) at another high for the year of $88.00/bbl, implying an extended period of high oil prices deep into 2027.

Whilst the European news was overwhelmingly negative, US equities put in a stronger performance, though the rally did lose some momentum as oil prices rebounded. The improvement was led by tech stocks, as the NASDAQ (+1.11%) had its best day in two weeks, and the Philly semiconductor index (+1.61%) finally ended a relentless run of 8 consecutive declines. So given the concentration of tech in the broader index, that actually helped the S&P 500 (+0.41%) to post a steady gain, even as almost two-thirds of components within the index lost ground on the day.

That AI stabilisation also pushed US Treasury yields higher, as it countered fears about an AI-related slowdown. Indeed, that was clear from the fact that higher real yields drove the bulk of the rise in Treasury yields yesterday, rather than inflation breakevens. So Treasury yields saw a consistent rise across the curve, with the 2yr yield (+6.5bps) up to 4.77%, whilst the 10yr yield (+6.6bps) rose to 5.14%. Moreover, that optimism on the growth side saw investors price in slightly more rate hikes for the months ahead. For instance, 74bps of hikes were priced in by the June 2027 meeting at the close, up +7.7bps relative to Friday.

As mentioned up top, the AI trade has reversed back again this morning with the KOSPI (-4.39%) leading the declines, dragged down by chip heavyweight SK hynix Inc. (-5.17%), which is on track for its lowest close since April. The Nikkei 225 (-1.08%) is also being weighed down by tech. Elsewhere, the Hang Seng (-0.95%) is also falling after reopening following a holiday, while China’s CSI 300 (-0.51%) is also soft. Additionally, the S&P/ASX 200 (-0.40%) is also edging lower with National Australia Bank (NAB) shares sliding around -3.0% after the lender announced restructuring charges and job cuts. Meanwhile, S&P 500 futures are up marginally (+0.06%), with Nasdaq 100 futures slipping (-0.20%) along with the overnight tech retreat. Stoxx (-0.60%) futures are continuing Europe's recent declines and 10yr USTs are -2.1bps lower standing at 5.12% as we go to print.

On the monetary policy front, the PBOC held its one-year and five-year Loan Prime Rates (LPR) steady at 3.00% and 3.50%, respectively. This marks the 17th consecutive month of unchanged benchmark rates, as stronger-than-expected Q3 GDP growth reduced the immediate need for monetary stimulus. While the decision provides no fresh rate relief for borrowers, the PBOC is reportedly considering replacing its seven-day reverse repo rate with the overnight rate as its primary policy benchmark to enhance monetary transmission.

Finally yesterday, there was little data to speak of. However, Canada’s CPI came in slightly softer than expected, with headline CPI only up to +3.1% in September (vs. +3.2% expected). Moreover, both of the core measures followed by the Bank of Canada unexpectedly fell by a tenth. So the median core measure fell to +1.9% (vs. +2.0% expected), and the trim core measure fell to +1.8%. Elsewhere, the US NAHB’s housing market index fell more than expected to 29 in October (vs. 31 expected), its lowest level since 2012.

Looking at the day ahead now, and data releases include UK unemployment for August, US housing starts, building permits and German PPI for September, and the German ZEW survey for October. Otherwise, central bank speakers include the BoE’s Greene. Finally, today’s earnings releases include Netflix, United Airlines and General Motors.

Two Tankers On Fire Off Oman As IRGC Boasts Of Naval Mine Warfare

On Tuesday the UK Maritime Operations Centre has reported a new incident around 121 nautical miles east of the Omani coast.

The UKMTO announced the vessel was "subject to interaction as part of ongoing military activity in the region" at around 10am GMT. Regional reports say two tankers are on fire. But Tehran is boasting of a fresh sea mine attack, amid daily ramped-up assaults on international shipping as it tries to hold on to leverage over the United States and global oil transit.

The Iranian side filled in more information, with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) describing that "Two violating oil tankers were set ablaze and halted due to the explosion of mines planted by the brave sailors of the IRGC Navy at an illegal crossing point in the southern part of the Strait of Hormuz," according to a statement published on their official Sepah News website.

This past weekend Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said that his country's offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on the table.

Mediation efforts said that "Qatar and Pakistan presented a 'compromise proposal' that meets the demands of both the American and Iranian sides", Al Araby Al Jadeed reports citing sources.

Those conditions were first presented in mid-September. "Our situation is clear and based on ⁠the seven-days proposal presented to the US. They shared comments which we are reviewing, but our proposal is still on the table and if there is any honesty on the US part, which there isn't, the way to reopening the Strait of Hormuz is obvious," Araqchi stated Sunday.

For anyone who has lost track, these are the seven conditions Tehran presented in September:

  1. lift the maritime blockade;
  2. restore Iran's frozen assets;
  3. lift sanctions on Iranian oil exports;
  4. halt all US actions "under the pretext of threats and military operations";
  5. end the war on Iran and its regional allies;
  6. withdraw US forces from areas around Iran's borders;
  7. pay compensation for war damage and commit not to interfere with Iran's nuclear and missile capabilities.

title: Charles Schwab, JPMorgan Restrict Third-Party AI Agents Over Security Risk
desc:
Charles Schwab, JPMorgan Restrict Third-Party AI Agents Over Security Risk

Authored by Bill Pan via The Epoch Times,

Some of Wall Street's largest financial firms are blocking third-party artificial intelligence agents from directly accessing customer accounts or moving money, citing concerns about security, control, and accountability if an autonomous system makes a mistake.

Charles Schwab, which reported $13.3 trillion in client assets at the end of the third quarter, is one of the latest firms to draw that line.

"We are blocking unauthorized agents who try to log in on behalf of clients," President and CEO Rick Wurster told analysts on Oct. 14 during Schwab's third-quarter earnings call.

The concern is not AI itself, he said, but outside agents using a customer's credentials and operating inside Schwab's systems without controls imposed by the brokerage.

Instead, Schwab plans to give third-party AI models a controlled way to connect via Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.

MCP allows an AI system to interact with outside data and services through defined permissions. Under Schwab's approach, an outside AI model could potentially retrieve information such as account balances or investment research while being blocked from higher-risk actions, including moving money.

Schwab is also rolling out its own generative AI assistant, Charley, which can answer questions and perform certain administrative tasks on customers' behalf.

Schwab is not alone. JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has confirmed that the bank will not allow just any outside AI agent into its systems to protect customers and the bank.

"You don't want rogue agents, and there could be thousands of them," Dimon said during an Oct. 13 earnings call.

A "rogue" agent generally refers to an AI system that takes actions outside the boundaries intended by its user or developer while pursuing its assigned goal.

Dimon also warned customers that if they're giving third-party AI agents access to their bank accounts, they're owning that decision.

"There's a liability transfer. They should understand the liability transfer," he said. "If data is being misused, they should understand it's being misused."

Could AI Move Deposits Faster?

Beyond cybersecurity, autonomous AI could also change the economics of banking.

Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Sløk warned in September that increasingly capable financial assistants could eventually create what he called an "agentic bank run."

Unlike a traditional bank run, in which customers withdraw money out of fear that a bank might fail, an agentic bank run could be driven by software that constantly seeks higher returns.

An AI assistant, for example, could continually compare interest rates and automatically move a household's cash from a low-yield checking account into higher-paying alternatives.

Apollo noted that some fintech and online accounts were offering yields ranging from 3.3 percent to 5 percent, compared with a national average of roughly 0.1 percent for checking accounts.

If AI made moving money nearly frictionless, Sløk argued, banks could lose some of the inexpensive deposits they rely on to fund loans.

Not every bank executive believes that prospect is happening any soon.

In an Oct. 13 earnings call, Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf said the idea of an AI-driven exodus to higher-yielding alternatives was "completely overdone."

"High-rate alternatives exist today. They've existed for a long time," Scharf told analysts. "If you want to move to a high rate, you can just go online and do it yourself in no time. That's not something new."

Who Is Liable When an AI Agent Goes Rogue?

Concerns about giving AI systems greater autonomy have been heightened by a series of cybersecurity incidents this year.

In July, ChatGPT developer OpenAI disclosed that a group, or "swarm," of its AI agents had broken out of restrictions within a testing environment and compromised the systems of Hugging Face, an online platform widely used by AI developers.

Separately, OpenAI apologized to the Australian government in September after one of its AI models infiltrated Australian government websites during a training exercise.

There is no single federal law that comprehensively assigns liability between an AI developer, the company deploying the system, and the user when an autonomous agent causes damage. Existing laws may apply depending on the circumstances.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has argued against giving AI developers broad immunity from liability.

"What we shouldn't do on safety is to give these labs a liability exemption, which is what they are asking for," Bessent said while testifying before the House Financial Services Committee on Sept. 15.

"The best way to guarantee safety is that the creators are liable for what they build and generate."

Earlier this month, Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) introduced the bipartisan AI Agent Accountability Act, aimed specifically at hacking carried out by AI agents.

Under the proposal, operators could face civil and criminal liability under federal computer-crime law if they knowingly operate an AI agent that recklessly causes hacking-related damage or loss.

Developers could also be held liable if they knew an agent was capable of hacking but failed to implement reasonable safeguards.

The bill would also allow the U.S. attorney general and state attorneys general to seek court orders against certain AI-agent hacking activity.

title: Saudi Arabia Executes Two Foreigners Over 'Indecent Acts' Inside Mecca Mosque

Bangladesh is seeking answers on why Saudi Arabia executed two Bangladeshi nationals in the city of Mecca - which is considered holy in Islam - without telling Dhaka.

Last week, Saudi Arabia executed a male and a female Bangladeshi national after they were convicted of committing "indecent acts" inside a mosque (in Mecca).

Riyadh did not provide further details on the acts the two Bangladeshi nationals allegedly committed or whether they had legal representation in the Gulf kingdom, according to local media reports.

Reacting to the incident, Bangladesh’s minister for foreign affairs, Humaiun Kobir, told reporters that he was "very disappointed" by the lack of communication and that Dhaka was seeking an explanation on why they were executed and not informed beforehand about the execution.

"We have sought an explanation from our friendly bilateral partner to look into the matter and know why the gap in information sharing and exchanges happened here. We are in discussions," he told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday.

Earlier, the Bangladeshi foreign ministry said that it was waiting for a copy of the full verdict and the circumstances that led to the execution.

The official added that the two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh but did not indicate that they had planned to execute them.

Last week, Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court overturned the death sentence of a Sri Lankan national after he allegedly insulted Islam and the Prophet Muhammad.

Sri Lanka’s Deputy Foreign Minister Arun Hemachandra confirmed that Riyadh had overturned the death sentence of Anojan Sivarasa.

The 27-year-old remains imprisoned after he was sentenced to five years in prison and fined three million Saudi Riyals ($800,000).

The court handed down the sentence amid intense criticism of Riyadh's legal system.

Saudi Arabia relies on interpretations of Islamic law, alongside cybercrime and counterterror legislation, to target online expression under the guise of protecting "public morals".

desc:
Alberta Overwhelmingly Votes To Stay In Canada In Historic Referendum

Alberta Voters Reject Separation From Canada as Carney Wins

With about 1.2 million votes counted, about 76% were in favor of remaining in Canada, enough for the Canadian Broadcasting Corp. to project victory for that side. The other option on the ballot was to support starting a legal process that could eventually lead to a second referendum on independence.

Premier Danielle Smith called the referendum in May after separatist organizers collected hundreds of thousands of names on a petition that asked for a vote. She advocated for staying in the country, though opinion surveys showed supporters of her United Conservative Party are divided on the matter. That tension may play out in the coming months, as she and others have warned of a potential split within the governing party.

"I'm very pleased to see the initial results from Elections Alberta show widespread support for remaining in Canada. Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada," Smith said in a statement. She said she would make a live address to the province on Tuesday evening.

The resource-rich province of 5 million people produces more than 4 million barrels a day of oil and ships the bulk of it to refineries in the US, helping to make energy Canada's largest category of exports. The region has been the epicenter of anger about former Prime Minister Justin Trudeau's environmental policies, which restricted energy development and sought to promote renewables over fossil fuels.

Since taking power more than 18 months ago, Carney has reversed or changed a number of Trudeau's signature policies - canceling a consumer carbon tax, loosening emissions rules and focusing the government on attracting more investment.

The prime minister, who grew up in Alberta, also made a series of pacts with Smith. title: Why Cheaper Restaurant Food May Stay Off The Menu This Year
desc:
Why Cheaper Restaurant Food May Stay Off The Menu This Year

Dining out is likely to remain expensive as uneven relief in ingredient costs keeps restaurant margins under pressure.

Lower cattle prices have provided some relief this past summer, but soaring cooking-oil and grain costs, along with a rebound in chicken prices, leave little room for broad menu price cuts, according to a note from BofA restaurant analyst Sara Senatore on Friday.

Cattle prices fell 9% from a year earlier in the third quarter, reversing a 9.8% increase in the second quarter, Senatore wrote. But the futures market points to a 1.4% rise from a year earlier in the fourth quarter and a 3.9% rise from the preceding three months.

The decline in cattle prices comes as major restaurant operators face elevated prices for a wide variety of inputs. Soybean oil prices rose 35.7% in the third quarter, while wheat gained 19.6% and corn increased 10%.

Chicken prices are also turning higher after a sharp decline over the last year. Breast prices were up 4% from October a year earlier, compared with a 36% decline in July. Wing prices rose 2%, reversing a 28% drop over the same period.

Impacts vary across restaurant chains. Beef and chicken account for 25% to more than 35% of food input costs at restaurants outside categories such as pizza, coffee, and desserts.

Texas Roadhouse sits at the higher end of protein exposure because its menu is mostly beef-based, while Cava and Sweetgreen sit at the lower end. These are the key restaurants Senatore covers.

Consumers hoping for relief from expensive restaurant bills may have to keep waiting. Senatore's mixed commodity outlook gives operators little reason to think that cost pressures are over.

title: Toyota's "Next Gen" Corolla Built In China Will Offer Multiple Powertrains
desc:
Toyota's "Next Gen" Corolla Built In China Will Offer Multiple Powertrains

Toyota is taking a more flexible approach to electrification, preparing to launch a redesigned Corolla in China in 2028 that can be manufactured with gasoline, hybrid or fully electric powertrains, according to Nikkei Asia. The move comes as automakers increasingly rethink their EV strategies amid slowing growth, fierce competition and uncertainty about how quickly consumers will abandon combustion engines.

Nikkei writes that the new Corolla will be built through Toyota's FAW joint venture using a multipathway platform designed to streamline manufacturing and reduce costs. Rather than committing to a single propulsion technology, Toyota will be able to adjust production based on consumer demand and market conditions.

The shift comes as Toyota struggles in China, where August sales fell 23% year over year to 118,449 vehicles, including Lexus. Domestic competition has intensified, pricing pressure has increased and profitability has suffered. Toyota is also developing longer-range Lexus EVs and extended-range electric vehicles that use gasoline engines to generate electricity.

More broadly, the global EV industry has experienced a significant reality check over the last several years. After an initial wave of enthusiasm fueled by government subsidies, ambitious emissions targets and aggressive manufacturer forecasts, EV adoption has become increasingly uneven. Sales continue to grow globally, particularly in China, but demand in several Western markets has fallen short of earlier expectations, prompting automakers to delay investments, scale back production targets and reconsider plans to eliminate combustion engines entirely.

Companies that once promised an almost exclusively electric future are increasingly embracing hybrids and other transitional technologies. High vehicle prices, charging infrastructure limitations, changing government incentives and consumer concerns about range have complicated the transition. Toyota's latest strategy reflects a growing recognition across the industry that the future of transportation may involve a broader mix of technologies than many manufacturers anticipated just a few years ago.

title: German Power Supply Startups Exit Market As Wholesale Prices Soar
desc:
German Power Supply Startups Exit Market As Wholesale Prices Soar

Authored by Michael Kern via OilPrice,

Two startup electricity retailers in Germany have recently announced they would cease operations as spiking wholesale prices amid the gas price surge are pressuring the industry again, and this time the pressure is compounded by plans for renewable policy changes.

Renewable electricity provider Grüüün, part of Münch Energie Group, early this month said it would discontinue servicing about 200,000 residential customers as of October 31, 2026, and these will now have to switch to other providers.

Grüüün, which launched operations in 2024, attributed its decision to fold to Germany's proposed changes to its renewable energy policy, including the upcoming overhaul of the Renewable Energy Sources Act (EEG 2027), the government's focus on gas-fired power generation, and rising grid charges that have disrupted its long-term pricing structure.

Another startup, Berlin-based Stromee, has also reportedly exited the German retail market after a local utility in western Germany, SWK Energie GmbH, said this week that it had taken over power and gas customers "in the low five-digit range."

The wholesale power price spikes and the regulatory shifts in Germany have made the sector vulnerable, with market exits reminiscent of the 2022 energy crisis when numerous small providers were forced to fold, Bloomberg notes.

This year, Germany is also facing the start of the winter with historically low levels of gas in storage sites. As of October 15, Germany's gas storage sites were 60% full, well below the EU average of 74%, according to data by Gas Infrastructure Europe. The EU storage levels are at their lowest since at least 2011, raising concerns that a cold winter could lead to gas shortages.

Thanks to diversified import capabilities, Germany doesn't face a gas supply shortage despite record-low levels of natural gas in storage sites, one of the biggest German gas importers, VNG, said at the end of last month.

Low stockpiles in Germany's vast storage, the world's fourth-largest, have prompted concerns about supply security if the coming winter turns out much colder than previous winters.

title: Shocker: Teens Put Down Their Phones For Summer Camp, Mental Health Improves
desc:
Shocker: Teens Put Down Their Phones For Summer Camp, Mental Health Improves

For two to three-and-a-half weeks, teenagers at a Maine summer camp traded their devices for outdoor activities and face-to-face friendships. By the end, their mental health had improved - with the largest gains among those who arrived struggling.

The findings add to research suggesting that relief from constant connectivity can produce benefits surprisingly quickly. They also raise a question - How much of it depends on what replaces the screen?

The study, published in Mental Health & Prevention, assessed 192 adolescents attending a device-free residential camp. Researchers included scientists from Sapien Labs and UC San Diego.

Participants' composite mental-health scores improved by an average of 10.1 points between arrival and departure. Those starting with mental-health struggles recorded a median improvement of 27 points. These are changes on the study's questionnaire scale, not percentage improvements or evidence that a psychiatric condition was cured.

The strongest gains involved adaptability and resilience. Campers also reported better focus and less worry and restlessness. Forty-four percent said they felt a stronger sense of belonging at camp than at school; 40% found making friends easier.

A session cost $4,900 to $7,900. Fewer than one in 10 campers arrived in the study's distressed or struggling range, against more than half of US teens on the same measure, and nearly a quarter saw their scores fall by more than five points. Sapien notes that there was no control group - so we can't know for sure whether removing devices caused the improvement, vs. how much came from exercise, sleep, friendship and the broader camp experience.

That said, there's been similar research...

A 2024 Danish study in JAMA Network Open randomly assigned 89 families, including 181 children and adolescents, either to reduce recreational screen use or continue their usual habits. For two weeks, the intervention families handed over smartphones and tablets and were instructed to limit leisure screen use to three hours per week per person. Basic phones preserved calls and texting.

Children in those families showed greater improvement in behavioral difficulties, particularly emotional symptoms and peer problems, alongside better prosocial behavior. The overall effect was moderate by conventional statistical standards.

This provides stronger evidence that changing screen habits can help. Still, the children averaged roughly nine years old, parents knew which group they were in and supplied the behavioral ratings, and the experiment did not establish whether the benefits were lasting.

In a 2014 study led by UCLA researchers, 51 sixth-graders spent five days at an outdoor camp without screens. Compared with 54 schoolmates who continued their normal routines, campers improved more at recognizing emotions from facial expressions and other nonverbal cues. That measured a social skill, rather than depression or anxiety. The groups were not randomly assigned, and outdoor activities and greater personal interaction accompanied the screen break. Nevertheless, the finding suggests that even a brief change in daily habits can affect how children read other people.

A 2025 randomized trial in PNAS Nexus enrolled 467 people in an experiment blocking internet access on their smartphones for two weeks. Calls, texts and internet access through other devices remained available. Researchers found improvements in mental health, wellbeing and objectively tested sustained attention. Participants reported spending more time socializing in person, exercising and being outdoors. Just 119 participants met the prespecified compliance threshold of keeping the block active for at least 10 days. The average participant was 32, so these results cannot simply be transferred to teenagers.

There is also emerging evidence from the Maine camp itself. A September 2026 preprint examined brain-wave recordings from 30 campers and reported changes associated with some improvements in wellbeing. However, it was a small, uncontrolled pilot, had not been peer-reviewed, and came from the same broader camp project. Meanwhile, a 2025 SMART Schools study compared 1,227 adolescents across 30 English schools. Students at schools with restrictive phone policies used phones less during school, but did not report better mental wellbeing. Their overall weekday and weekend phone use was not significantly different.

Maine campers who said they exercised more at camp gained 17.4 points on average, against 4.8 for those who exercised less. Those who felt a stronger sense of belonging gained 15 points, against 5.8 for those whose sense of belonging fell. None of those gaps reached statistical significance, and the scores were taken on the last day of camp, so whether the gains lasted after campers went home is unknown.

title: European Parliament Condemns Muslim Brotherhood, Calls For Crackdown on Islamist Influence
desc:
European Parliament Condemns Muslim Brotherhood, Calls For Crackdown on Islamist Influence

Authored by AG News Staff via American Greatness,

The European Parliament has approved a resolution condemning the Muslim Brotherhood and calling for stronger action against Islamist influence in European institutions. The resolution is a significant development in the continent's efforts to combat political extremism.

The center-right European People's Party spearheaded the resolution, which follows the Trump administration's designation of the Muslim Brotherhood and four affiliated branches as terrorist organizations.

French European Parliament member Céline Imart, who sponsored the measure, celebrated the vote as a breakthrough.

"This is a historic victory because it is a European first," Imart said, describing the resolution as Europe's first parliamentary action specifically confronting Islamist infiltration and the Muslim Brotherhood.

The resolution warns that organized Islamist networks threaten democratic institutions, religious freedoms, the rule of law and equality between men and women.

It calls for greater scrutiny of foreign funding, particularly involving organizations connected to Qatar and Turkey, and increased transparency surrounding European Union funding of groups suspected of Muslim Brotherhood ties.

Lawmakers also urged the European Council to consider whether Brotherhood-linked individuals and organizations should be added to the EU's terrorist list.

Lorenzo Vidino, director of George Washington University's Program on Extremism, said conservative lawmakers overwhelmingly supported the measure, while significant portions of the political left opposed it.

Imart criticized socialist and far-left lawmakers for boycotting negotiations on the resolution.

Security experts described the vote as an important first step toward confronting Islamist organizations accused of exploiting European democratic institutions.

"This resolution is where the pushback begins against Islamist entryism in Europe," said Edmund Fitton-Brown, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.

However, the European Network Against Racism condemned the resolution, calling it discriminatory and warning that it could unfairly target Muslim communities and civil society organizations.

The Parliament emphasized that protecting Muslims from discrimination remains essential while distinguishing religious freedom from organized Islamist political activity.

Unlike the Trump administration's terrorist designations, the European resolution is not binding legislation. Additional action by EU institutions would be required to implement its recommendations.

Imart vowed to continue pressing European leaders to act.

"This vote is a victory, but it is also a starting point," she said.

title: Veterans Blast 'Palestine Poppy' As Hijacking Of Remembrance Symbol, A Week After Protesters Trampled Battle Of Britain Wreaths
desc:
Veterans Blast 'Palestine Poppy' As Hijacking Of Remembrance Symbol, A Week After Protesters Trampled Battle Of Britain Wreaths

Pro-Palestinian campaigners are selling a "Palestine Poppy" in the green, red, white and black of the Palestinian flag ahead of Remembrance Sunday, and British veterans say it hijacks the country's day of mourning for its war dead, GB News reports.

The badge is on eBay for £1.74 each, and the Mail counts more than 1,200 sold so far. The group behind it calls the poppies "a symbol of solidarity and remembrance for the ongoing struggle of the Palestinian people and their fight for justice." Sales are not-for-profit, with a "small donation" going to charities in Palestine and to groups seeking to end "the occupation and war crimes through legal routes."

Retired Army officer and defense analyst Lt. Col. Stuart Crawford told GB News the badge is an attempt to "ride on the coat-tails of the familiar red poppy."

"The Remembrance poppy is avowedly apolitical," he said, while the Palestine version is "unashamedly political, designed to divide rather than unite."

Former Royal Navy officer Stuart Fawcett tied it to last weekend's march in London.

"Now, we see them hijacking our national symbol of remembrance," he told the broadcaster.

The march he means took place Saturday, Oct. 10. The Met Police said it made 20 arrests, six of them for criminal damage after protesters climbed the Battle of Britain memorial on the Embankment, where wreaths at the base were trampled and destroyed. Others were held for showing placards backing Palestine Action, a proscribed group, and for a racially aggravated public order offense after a woman was seen making a Nazi salute, Jewish News reports, citing the force.

Conservative MP Nick Timothy called the protesters "scum," and Lord Hannan asked what they had against the Battle of Britain pilots. Deputy Assistant Commissioner Carl Galvin, who ran the operation, said the march's timing near the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 attack raised the risk to community relations.

The poppy's website carries the slogan "From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free," which critics read as a denial of Israel's right to exist, the Mail notes. It also calls those killed or displaced in Gaza victims of "genocide," a label Israel and its supporters reject.

title: Is Turkiye Plotting A Coup In Brotherly Azerbaijan?
desc:
Is Turkiye Plotting A Coup In Brotherly Azerbaijan?

Authored by Andrew Korybko via Substack,

A now-deleted Azeri article over the weekend, whose initial publication was perceived by many Turks as having been state-approved, prompted a complaint from the Turkish Embassy in Baku and worsened mutual suspicions among these fraternal people of what the other's government is up to.

The Turkish Embassy in Baku released a statement over the weekend denying a local media report that former spy chief-turned-Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan's picture with members of the "Youth Assistance Foundation" during his latest trip to Baku to attend a multilateral event was proof of a secret meeting. The report has since been deleted, but the gist was that the aforesaid group and others are operating under Turkiye's influence to weaponize the recent pro-hijab protests for regime change purposes.

For background, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's condemnation of unnamed states' hijab bans in his UNGA speech last month preceded the entry into force of Azerbaijan's new school uniform policy that was interpreted by some administrators in that way, thus prompting a wave of protests. His Azerbaijani counterpart Ilham Aliyev then accused unnamed states of meddling in Azeri affairs during a speech to members of the ruling party. Some Azeris suspect that Turkish activists organized the protests.

Ahead of the previously mentioned event in Baku, Aliyev dispatched his national airline to pick up his Israeli counterpart on a plane named after the Azeri-Turkish alliance to fly him to to Baku across Turkish airspace despite Ankara banning all Israeli flights, which some Turks considered to be a snub. Since then, critical articles about Turkiye have appeared in Azeri media, which is considered by some to be state-influenced. This further fueled their ongoing social media disputes. Here are three background briefings:

* 5 October: "The Azeri-Turkish Brotherhood Is Going Through Some Trouble"

* 14 October: "The Azeri-Turkish Brotherhood Is Being Tested By Azerbaijan's Pro-Hijab Protests"

* 17 October: "Aliyev Used Israeli President Herzog To Take Three Jabs At Erdogan"

Two driving forces are behind this unprecedented dispute between these fraternal nations that consider themselves to be "one nation, two states". These are Turkiye's discomfort with Azerbaijan's de facto alliance with Israel, with which Turkiye has been in a rivalry since October 7th, and Azerbaijan's discomfort what some perceive to be Turkiye's Neo-Ottoman plans. Some Turks now suspect that Israel is behind Azerbaijan's alleged hijab ban while some Azeris suspect that Turkiye is behind the protests.

Moreover, some Azeris worry that Turkiye's suspected plans to turn August 2025's "Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity" into a Turkish-led NATO logistics corridor along Russia's southern periphery could spark a Ukrainian-like war, while some Turks believe that Israel planted these fears. The hijab issue was therefore only the spark for getting Azeris and Turks to air out their grievances against one another on social media, not the root cause, but it now seems to have taken on a life of its own.

This background contextualizes the earlier cited article that was deleted after the Turkish Embassy's complaint. While its veracity is unclear, what's much more certain is that its publication was probably greenlit to signal to Turkiye to rein in its social media activists who've directly involved themselves in Azerbaijan's hijab debate, which Baku tacitly considers to be meddling given the protests that have since followed. If they don't soon stop, then Azeris might consider this to be a betrayal of their brotherhood.

desc:
My Grandmother's "Just-In-Case" Cupboard Doesn't Look So Eccentric Anymore

Authored by Madge Waggy via A lot will happen in 2026!,

My grandmother kept a cupboard she called the just-in-case, and for most of my childhood I read it as a harmless eccentricity rather than what it was - a wound made edible. She had been a girl during the Depression, and somewhere in her twenties she had learned to keep tinned beans, sacks of flour, jars sealed with wax and paper, all of it rotated with the humourless discipline of a quartermaster provisioning for a war that had already ended but might, at any hour, resume. Nothing in that cupboard was ever eaten first. It sat at the back of the shelf like a private insurance policy against a world that had once taken everything from her family and could, she believed, do so again at a moment's notice.

For years the cupboard looked like a relic. The country around it grew fat. Food in America became cheap in a way that no other civilisation in history had ever managed, cheap enough that a family could throw away a third of what it bought and call it a lifestyle, cheap enough that the word hunger retreated into the vocabulary of charity drives and faraway places. We built an entire national identity on the assumption that the shelves would always be full, that the price would always be bearable, that the great problem of food would remain a problem of excess rather than of want. To doubt that assumption in the middle of the nineties was to be faintly embarrassing, like a man who keeps a shotgun in a suburb.

Then the erosion began, and it began so quietly that it registered less as a crisis than as a mood. A receipt that used to total forty dollars now totals sixty and buys less. A bag of chips feels lighter in the hand. A cut of beef that was once a weekly habit becomes a monthly occasion, and nobody announces the change because there is nothing to announce - the change simply happens, and the new state of things becomes the baseline against which the next change will be measured. This is the particular cruelty of slow decline: it is always, at any given moment, almost bearable, and so it is never quite urgent enough to resist.

What follows is an attempt to take the temperature of that decline, using what can be measured and admitting plainly where measurement fails. The argument is not that America is about to re-enter 1932, with soup kitchens on every corner and men in cloth caps hiding their faces in a breadline. The argument is subtler and, in some ways, more disturbing - that the country is sliding back toward the conditions that produced the Depression diet, that the slide is visible now to anyone who bothers to look at a scale, a price tag, or an empty shelf, and that the most likely future is not collapse but a long, grinding narrowing in which abundance survives as an appearance while it dies as a reality.

🩸 What the Register Confesses

Begin where every household begins, at the point of sale, because that is where the first symptoms surface and where the official figures are quietly outstripped by what people actually pay. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that grocery prices rose by roughly 2.9 percent over the twelve months to September 2026, with overall food inflation running near 2.5 percent, and a government forecast for the coming year of about three percent - numbers that arrive in the newspapers as reassurance. The reassurance is largely an artefact of averaging. A three-percent basket is composed of items that fell, items that held, and items that detonated, and the shopper does not buy an average; the shopper buys the specific things a household needs, and the things a household needs have a habit of being the things that detonated.

Beef is the clearest case, and it deserves the attention it gets because it is the load-bearing protein of the working table. Ground beef, the cheapest way a family can put red meat on a plate, climbed roughly 18.9 percent year over year, averaging near $6.75 a pound, while a pound of steak approached $12.80 by May 2026 - prices that would have read as a butcher's fantasy a decade earlier. The Department of Agriculture expects beef and veal to rise another five to nine percent through the year, depending on which forecast you trust, and the reasons are structural rather than temporary, which is to say the reasons will not politely go away when the news cycle turns. Coffee, meanwhile, has risen about 55 percent since February 2024, a fact that lands harder when you remember that almost no coffee is grown domestically and the entire supply depends on weather and politics thousands of miles away. Lettuce added 39 percent over a comparable stretch, sirloin steak 21 percent, orange juice 15 percent, and the small consolations - sweets, biscuits, the cheap sugar that a household reaches for when everything savoury has become expensive - are forecast to climb close to seven percent in 2026 alone.

  • Ground beef: up roughly 18.9 percent year over year, averaging near $6.75 a pound.
  • Coffee: up about 55 percent since February 2024, with a 50 percent tariff on Brazilian beans layered on top.
  • Lettuce: up 39 percent; sirloin steak up 21 percent; orange juice up 15 percent.
  • Sugar and confectionery: forecast to rise nearly 7 percent in 2026.
  • Imported pasta: pushed upward by a tariff that has reached 107 percent.
  • Cocoa: more than doubled since 2024 as West African harvests fail.

Underneath the headline items sits the tariff layer, which the shopper rarely sees and invariably pays. A levy on Brazilian coffee, a punitive rate on European pasta, duties scattered across imported cheese, olive oil, seafood and out-of-season produce - each one is small enough to be invisible on its own, and together they form a quiet surcharge on the entire act of eating. Add to this the slower pressures that no policy can reverse quickly: drought driving up the cost of feed, ranchers reducing herds because they cannot afford to keep them, and a rebuilding cycle measured in years rather than months. None of it is a cliff. All of it is a slope, and the slope tilts the same way every month.
