title: Supreme Showdown: Investigative Reporter And Accused Chinese Operative Face Off In Press Freedom Case
desc:
Supreme Showdown: Investigative Reporter And Accused Chinese Operative Face Off In Press Freedom Case

Authored by Jonathan Turley via JonathanTurley.org,

Below is my column in The Hill on an important case currently before the Supreme Court on the free press and the ability to protect confidential sources. The underlying facts may seem like something out of The Onion: an accused Chinese operative and PLA Colonel who was viewed as a national security risk is successfully using the Privacy Act to get a respected journalist to reveal her confidential sources. However, it is very serious and, unless the Court reviews the case, investigative journalism in the United States could suffer a debilitating blow with little more than a shrug from the courts.

Here is the column:

This month, journalist Catherine Herridge is in the fight of her life - and the stakes for the country could not be higher. The former Fox and CBS reporter has long been one of the most prominent investigative journalists in the U.S., particularly on national security stories. She is now on her last appeal to the Supreme Court, attempting to protect the most vital prerequisite of the free press: confidentiality of sources.

At issue is a 2017 story that aired on Fox News concerning a Virginia-based training firm patronized by Pentagon officials. Herridge exposed ties of the University of Management and Technology to the Chinese military. It was the kind of difficult, complex story that made Herridge such a respected figure in her profession. The subject of the story, University of Management and Technology founder Yanping Chen, sued, claiming that the exposure had led to her loss of employment.

Such lawsuits are usually brought against journalists by disgruntled subjects under defamation or other grounds that are quickly dismissed by courts. But Chen brought a novel claim against various officials under the Privacy Act. She alleges that they disclosed to Herridge protected information about an FBI investigation. Rather than sue Herridge directly, Chen subpoenaed her to disclose the names of her sources. Herridge sat for a deposition but refused to breach confidentiality.

This is not Herridge's first rodeo in fighting for journalistic values. Years ago, CBS News forced her out and seized her files containing confidential source information. Despite considerable costs, Herridge eventually stared down the network and forced it to return the files.

Notably, much of the Fox News story about Chen was available in the public domain. For example, a whistleblower and FBI informant had said publicly that Chen had admitted to him that she had been a colonel in China's People's Liberation Army. He also alleged that she told him to lie about that fact when called to testify before a federal grand jury.

Because Herridge refuses to disclose her sources, we do not know how much she actually relied on non-public information. This puts her in an impossible position: She would have to reveal sources in order to show that Chen's claims are meritless.

In making her Privacy Act claim, Chen cited the disclosure of many facts already available publicly, including contradictions of her denials on being part of the Chinese military. The only information that had not already appeared in the public domain appears to be photographic, including a picture of Chen in a Chinese colonel's uniform.

In this case, Herridge had the misfortune of seeking relief in Washington, D.C., where judges have been relatively permissive in allowing such disputes to go to trial. In 2023, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, an Obama appointee, tossed aside protections that other circuit courts recognize under the First Amendment. He ordered Herridge to identify her confidential sources, then held her in contempt when she refused, imposing a crippling $800-a-day fine. Even that was not enough for Chen, who tried to have the penalties increased to $5,000 a day.

Before the fines were paused in August pending appeal, Herridge had to write a check every day from her two children's college funds. "These fines are designed to break you emotionally and professionally," she told me. "I would walk every day to the mailbox with our oldest son for emotional and moral support."

Unfortunately, a panel of three judges on the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld Cooper's ruling. Herridge therefore went to the Supreme Court for an emergency injunction against the daily fine. The court refused to intervene immediately, although Justice Brett Kavanaugh indicated that he wanted to grant the relief.

Herridge is now back before the Supreme Court, which will have a final opportunity to take the case and prevent a catastrophic blow to press freedoms. If the court again punts, then any aggrieved subject of a news story could effectively strip journalistic sources of confidentiality by alleging a Privacy Act violation.

The cause of this pileup is the highly permissive standard adopted by the D.C. Circuit for the single most important jurisdiction for investigative reporting. To compel disclosure, Chen needs only to show that the source is central to her case and that she has exhausted other avenues of discovery. This test exposes every reporter who breaks a story in Washington involving government abuse or waste. Imagine if Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein had been sued under the Privacy Act by Nixon administration officials and forced to disclose the identity of Deep Throat.

Other circuits have a balancing test that allows for a more contextual resolution of such disputes. Another approach would be to deny such compelled disclosures when the case (as here) would not likely survive a motion for summary judgment. Chen, who lost her position because of information already in the public domain, cannot possibly show meaningful injuries from these photographs.

The irony in the case is crushing. Chen is an alleged former colonel in the People's Liberation Army, using the U.S. Privacy Act to gut a Constitutional right not recognized in China. Of course she still has rights in this country, but the question is not whether she can sue under the Privacy Act - it is what standard she must meet before the courts make a journalist betray confidential sources.

Herridge got the story right and did the right thing in protecting her sources at great personal cost. The justices now have a chance to protect her. They should take her case. Not only has it created a split among the circuit courts, but it also has a compelling record to reconsider the confusing 1972 decision in Branzburg v. Hayes, which one appellate judge ridiculed for being "about as clear as mud."

Herridge is not seeking immunity or a favor. She is a tough reporter who just wants to do her job and protect her sources under a fair legal standard. The question is whether four justices will agree and grant review in Herridge v. Chen.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of "Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution." He previously worked for CBS News and currently works at Fox News as a legal analyst. His views do not necessarily reflect those of those networks.

title: Brookfield, NextEra To Build $100 Billion AI Hub On Cold War Nuclear Site
desc:
Brookfield, NextEra To Build $100 Billion AI Hub On Cold War Nuclear Site

Authored by Alex Kimani via OilPrice,

The U.S. Department of Energy (DoE) has announced a landmark $100-billion private investment to turn the former uranium enrichment site in Western Kentucky into the new Paducah American Energy Hub, marking one of the largest economic development projects in Kentucky's history.

Led by U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright, the initiative will bring together a private-sector coalition to build a massive artificial intelligence and high-performance computing (HPC) innovation campus powered by new energy infrastructure. The phased buildout is targeted for 2032, and is expected to create roughly 8,000 construction jobs and 600 permanent operations jobs. Brookfield Asset Management (NYSE:BAM) has been selected to build the 1.8-gigawatt (GW) AI and HPC data center campus while NextEra Energy (NYSE:NEE) will develop 2 GW of natural gas-fired generation coupled with 2.6 GW of battery energy storage. The project is designed to operate on dedicated power supplies capable of feeding excess energy back to the regional grid to avoid raising utility bills for local families and businesses. The campus will also deploy a modern closed-loop cooling system to continuously recirculate water and minimize external consumption. The project leaders emphasize that this design is vastly more resource-efficient compared to the site's previous tenant, the Cold War-era Paducah Gaseous Diffusion Plant, which was originally designed to pull up to 30 million gallons of water per day from the Ohio River.

Still, the Paducah project comes at a time when the market is souring on heavy AI infrastructure spending.

Last year, Trump, alongside Oracle's Larry Ellison, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SoftBank CEO Masayoshi Son, unveiled Stargate, a private-sector joint venture intended to invest up to $500 billion over four years to build hyper-scale AI data centers and energy infrastructure across the United States. Billed by Trump as the "largest AI infrastructure project in history," Stargate is designed to secure American dominance in AI over foreign competitors like China. Oracle serves as the core cloud and infrastructure provider for the venture. Initial development of the project began in Abilene, Texas, consisting of multiple 500,000-square-foot data center buildings to house the immense computing power needed for next-generation AI models.

Unfortunately, the ambitious AI infrastructure project found itself on the ropes just months after its grand launch.

Back in January, Business Insider reported that JPMorgan Chase was having trouble syndicating the $38 billion in construction debt it underwrote for the Stargate AI data center initiative as institutional investors grow increasingly cautious regarding concentrated tech sector exposure. Banks spent more than six months attempting to distribute the multi-billion-dollar debt packages for the Stargate campuses located in Texas and Wisconsin; however, buyers appeared uninterested in taking on massive piles of debt tied heavily to single-tenant AI operations. Oracle leases the facilities, and S&P cut Oracle in July to BBB-, one notch above junk, over its data center spending. Investors demanded a higher return to hold the debt, and the banks had to sell it at a discount.

In April, OpenAI officially paused its Stargate UK data center project, citing high industrial electricity prices and regulatory uncertainty. Stargate UK was planned in partnership with hardware firms Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Nscale, aiming to deploy thousands of advanced AI chips (starting with 8,000 GPUs and scaling up to 31,000) across sites in North-East England, including Cobalt Park near Newcastle and Blyth.

Whereas OpenAI did not cancel the project outright, the AI giant says it will only resume development only when the "right conditions" allow for long-term infrastructure investment. The pause dealt a major blow to UK infrastructure partner Nscale (founded by Josh Payne), which had been scaling up operations and weighing a potential stock market IPO, as well as Britain's push to emerge as a sovereign AI superpower.

The UK pause is the second blow to OpenAI's planned capacity in a month.

Last month, Bloomberg reported that Oracle's pivotal $18-billion Project Jupiter, a massive 1,400-acre data center campus in New Mexico critical to supporting the broader AI infrastructure goals, has stalled. Oracle issued a force majeure notice to lender Blue Owl Capital regarding the 2.45-gigawatt hyperscale data center in southern New Mexico after the tech giant failed to secure vital state and federal land-use permits for a planned natural gas plant. Instead, Oracle announced plans to shift over to solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs), an experimental stopgap that has never been deployed on a scale this large.

Public resistance to data centers has been growing rapidly across the United States, Europe and Asia as communities push back against the massive environmental and economic footprint of AI infrastructure. A recent Gallup poll shows that roughly 71% of Americans oppose the construction of AI data centers in their localities. Pushback in the U.S. has resulted in projects worth over $130 billion blocked or delayed, with reports indicating more than 500 active data center bans or moratoriums have popped up nationwide.

title: 'Once He Leaves, The Case Is Over': Judge Jails OpenAI Bugging Suspect After Saudi Consulate Offers 'Blank-Check' Bail
desc:
'Once He Leaves, The Case Is Over': Judge Jails OpenAI Bugging Suspect After Saudi Consulate Offers 'Blank-Check' Bail

When a foreign government volunteers to bankroll your release from federal custody, it may be time to reconsider the "no ties to a foreign state" defense.

On Monday, a San Francisco federal magistrate ordered Abdulrahman Alfozan, the 35-year-old Saudi national accused of bugging an executive conference room at OpenAI's headquarters, detained without bail pending trial, saying there is a "significant" risk he would flee. The ruling came after Judge Alex Tse grilled the defense over an offer by the Saudi Consulate in Los Angeles to pay Alfozan's full bail, which CNBC reports that the judge called "problematic".

In other words, the Kingdom offered to post bail for the man accused of bugging the room where OpenAI meets government officials, and the judge decided that was not, in fact, reassuring.

But, there's a lot more going on here...

"Problematic"

Alfozan's lawyer, William Pernik, had asked for release on home detention with GPS monitoring and a co-signed bond, backed by a written undertaking from the Saudi Consulate General. In court, the defense said Alfozan would also put up $1 million in assets on top of the consulate's offer. The defense package also came with dozens of support letters and a commitment from the consulate not to issue him travel documents.

Tse wasn't buying it. The judge noted that OpenAI had already fired Alfozan, so there is no job keeping him in the Bay Area, and ordered him back in court next month.

Courtroom accounts had the judge likening Riyadh's open-ended support to a "blank check", which is roughly the opposite of what you want a federal judge saying about your sureties.

“Even if I set it at $10 million, they are going to pay the entire bond," the judge reportedly said, adding that "there is a real threat here that once he leaves, the case is over."

Prosecutors from the Northern District of California had argued that Alfozan's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States" and that he enjoyed "considerable support" from the Saudi government.

The defense countered that nationality is not evidence of flight and that the planned trip was for family and immigration reasons. According to CBS, Alfozan has been a US permanent resident since September 2020 and had applied for citizenship,

"Saudi Needs You More Then The U.S.!"

The government's case for detention, filed Sunday, is where things got colorful. Prosecutors said Alfozan was in frequent WhatsApp contact with a member of the Saudi Royal Family throughout 2025 and 2026, as recently as Oct. 5, four days before his arrest. The royal (unnamed in the filing) told him about a new Saudi AI program and repeatedly pressed him on when he'd leave OpenAI. The May 2026 exchange is worth quoting from the filing directly:

"Saudi needs you more then [sic] the U.S.!"

Alfozan's reply: "100"

Translation: agreed. According to CBS, Alfozan added he wouldn't leave until his stock vested, which, in fairness, is the most relatable thing anyone in this story has said.

To be clear (and the defense will make this point at every opportunity), the filing does not allege the royal directed Alfozan to plant the device or steal anything from OpenAI. It also doesn't say how the two knew each other. But it does describe internal searches concerning meetings between OpenAI and Saudi officials: reports say Alfozan accessed an internal folder labeled "Saudi Gov Docs" and searched for a meeting tagged "HUMAIN x MCIT @OpenAI", a reference to the PIF-backed AI champion and the Kingdom's communications and IT ministry. Prosecutors also flagged that further charges could follow.

Regular readers will recall that HUMAIN is the vehicle through which Riyadh has been hoovering up US AI chips (May 14, 2025), with Washington signing off on advanced chip exports (Nov 20, 2025) as part of what we described as American AI imperialism's reliance on the Middle East (Jan 6, 2026). Turns out the reliance may run both ways.

Meanwhile, after his arrest derailed a family trip, prosecutors say the Saudi government and a Saudi military official each arranged flights out of the US for his wife, Lujain Alassaf, and their three-month-old son. That trip, recall, was a one-way booking to Saudi Arabia via Istanbul for Oct. 12, three days after the FBI picked him up, as first disclosed last week. Alfozan is also listed as a venture partner at Riyadh's Raed Ventures, whose partners include a member of the royal family; one former CIA official told CNBC the firm is basically an arm of the state.

Toilet Paper Tradecraft

As a reminder, the underlying case is one we covered when it broke last week. According to the DOJ complaint, OpenAI staff found an encrypted audio recorder wrapped in toilet paper and plugged into a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room on Sept. 30; it had been installed around Sept. 28.

OpenAI then added a camera, which on Oct. 5 caught Alfozan entering and checking behind the TV. The same day, security found a second recorder from the same Chinese manufacturer in a bag he'd left in a printer room - along with his wallet and ID.

The complaint also cited AI prompts about building, obfuscating, and remotely accessing a recorder, and says he used an internal productivity tool to map executive meeting rooms and leadership schedules. The room in question routinely hosted meetings between OpenAI executives and government officials, including on days close to when the device was allegedly planted. OpenAI said it has no indication that model weights, source code or customer data were accessed.

The charge itself - using or trying to use a device to intercept oral communications - carries a maximum of five years and a $250,000 fine (which, as prosecutors seem to appreciate, is a much smaller number than what a one-way ticket to Riyadh is worth).

Same Consulate, Same Offer, Different Ending

Why would a judge balk at a foreign consulate guaranteeing bail? Because this particular consulate has done it before.

In 2016, the Saudi Consulate in Los Angeles posted $100,000 in bail for Abdulrahman Sameer Noorah, a Portland Community College student charged with manslaughter in the hit-and-run death of 15-year-old Fallon Smart. His passport was confiscated and he wore a GPS ankle monitor. Two weeks before trial in June 2017, he cut it off and vanished, turning up in Saudi Arabia a week later, reportedly on a Saudi-issued passport under another name.

The Oregonian later tallied more than two dozen Saudi suspects who fled US charges, in several cases after Riyadh posted bail. And since there is no US-Saudi extradition treaty, Noorah has never been back.

Passport surrender, GPS monitoring, a consular guarantee: the exact package Alfozan's lawyers offered on Monday. We suspect Judge Tse has read The Oregonian.

Bottom Line

The timing is not lost on Washington. Late last week, DNI Jay Clayton - who called the OpenAI incident a "serious situation" - warned that the administration and US companies "need to be wary" of AI espionage, singling out China, Russia, Iran and North Korea.

But between the royal WhatsApps, the "Saudi Gov Docs" searches, the military-arranged flights for his family, and a consulate eager to cut a check, prosecutors don't need to prove motive to win a detention hearing - and they didn't.

The bigger question is what this does to the Gulf AI trade. Washington has spent two years waving through chip exports to Riyadh and Abu Dhabi on the premise that 'Gulf capital' is a partner in the US AI buildout, not a collector of its secrets. One alleged toilet-paper bug won't unwind those deals, but it hands every export-control hawk in Congress a brand-new exhibit - or, more likely, gets quietly filed under "isolated incident" the next time a HUMAIN megadeal needs a signature.

Tehran appointed a new Defense Minister, military industry veteran Mehrdad Akhlaghi, on Sunday during a vote of confidence at an open session of the Iranian parliament.

Akhlaghi received 237 votes in favor and 15 against, with no abstentions. Former Defense Minister Aziz Nasirzadeh was killed in US-Israeli strikes at the start of the illegal war in February.

After his killing, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian appointed Seyed Majid Ebn al-Reza as acting defense minister until Akhlaghi was voted in on Sunday.

The new defense minister had worked exclusively on military and weapons research for several years before entering the defense industry sector, where he began subsequently managing research and production activities at the same time, according to WANA.

Akhlaghi previously served as the managing director of the Islamic Republic’s Aerospace Industries Organization. He also headed Iran’s Defense Industries Organization.

He says the missile and drone programs are a major part of his military expansion plan.

Akhlaghi promised the ministry would pursue extensive drone research and production over the next 22 months.

Additionally, he vowed an expansion of aerospace and satellite technology. "We must build our military satellites ourselves and launch them ourselves," he said during parliamentary proceedings.

He outlined plans to advance an Iranian-developed heavy fighter aircraft and expand and increase the outsourcing of defense manufacturing components.

The minister has also issued a stern warning against the US and Israel.

"People can rest assured that they will most likely not dare to attack us," he told reporters. "If [the US] do, they themselves and the region will suffer enormous damage."

“If the American enemy once again makes a miscalculation, the response of the brave Iranian nation and the Islamic Republic’s fighters will be surprising and extensive,” he went on to say.
